title: Something in the eye or a scratched eye

differential.label: Small particle on the eye or under the eyelid
differential.note: Working idea only. This is not a diagnosis. Floating debris is the most recorded eye problem in flight.

differential.label: Scratch on the clear front of the eye (corneal abrasion)
differential.note: Working idea only. This is not a diagnosis. Pain, tearing, light sensitivity and blurred vision can follow a scratch.

differential.label: Chemical in the eye. Emergency
differential.note: Working idea only. This is not a diagnosis. Flush first, then call the flight surgeon.

differential.label: Object stuck in the eye. Emergency
differential.note: Working idea only. This is not a diagnosis. Do not remove it. Needs flight surgeon review.

differential.label: Eye infection
differential.note: Working idea only. This is not a diagnosis. Needs flight surgeon review.

tests.title: Pain score
tests.instruction: Stay restrained. Enter a pain score from 0 to 10.

tests.title: Vision check, right eye
tests.instruction: Cover the left eye with your hand. Read the lowest line you can on the onboard eye chart. Write down the line.

tests.title: Vision check, left eye
tests.instruction: Cover the right eye with your hand. Read the lowest line you can on the onboard eye chart. Write down the line.

tests.title: Chemical check
tests.instruction: Ask what touched the eye. Note yes if any chemical, cleaning fluid or unknown liquid got in it.

immediateSteps.title: If a chemical got in the eye, flush it now
immediateSteps.instruction: Put on the eyewash goggles with the outflow side on the hurt eye. Flush the eye. Keep flushing for at least 15 minutes. Then call the flight surgeon.

immediateSteps.title: If something is stuck in the eye, leave it
immediateSteps.instruction: Do not pull it out. Do not press on it. Loosely cover both eyes. Call the flight surgeon now.

immediateSteps.title: Do not rub the eye
immediateSteps.instruction: Keep hands off the eye. Do not squeeze the eyelids.

immediateSteps.title: Clean your hands
immediateSteps.instruction: Wash or wipe your hands before you touch the eye or eyelid.

immediateSteps.title: Blink
immediateSteps.instruction: Blink several times. Tears often wash out tiny particles.

immediateSteps.title: Rinse with artificial tears
immediateSteps.instruction: Hold the bottle above the outer corner of the eye. Do not touch the eye with the tip. Let the drops run across the eye.

immediateSteps.title: Use the eyewash goggles if drops do not work
immediateSteps.instruction: Put on the eyewash goggles. Flush the eye. Keep the water inside the goggles.

immediateSteps.title: Check vision in each eye
immediateSteps.instruction: Do the vision check for each eye. Enter what you read.

immediateSteps.title: Send the case to the flight surgeon
immediateSteps.instruction: Continue to handoff and send the case. Say if vision changed.

cautions: This card is not a diagnosis. It gives no doses. Do not rub or press the eye. Keep eyewash water inside the goggles so it does not float into equipment. Long use of numbing eye drops can make eye injuries worse, so use them only as the flight surgeon directs. Use any kit item only as the flight surgeon directs.
sourceNote: Researcher card, Pulseframe Batch 1, 2026-11-15. Built from NASA IMM data, peer reviewed spaceflight ophthalmology reviews (Suh et al., Meer et al., npj Microgravity) and MedlinePlus first aid. Not a NASA procedure. The ISS medical checklist eye procedure is not public. Pending second-person safety review.
redFlagsLifeThreat: A chemical got in the eye.
Something is stuck in or through the eye.
Vision changed: blurred, double or lost.
Blood is pooling in the eye.
redFlagsCallGround: Pain or blurred vision continues after the particle is out.
The eye is painful and red.
Nausea or headache comes with the eye pain.
A scratchy feeling lasts more than a day or two.

timeLimits.item: Chemical in the eye: start flushing at once and keep flushing at least 15 minutes.
Minor scratchy feeling after a particle is removed should go away within a day or two. If not, call the flight surgeon.

whenGroundUnavailable.status: PARTIAL (historical rule found, no current rule)
whenGroundUnavailable.detail: The 2001 ISS medical checklist says that in an emergency or during loss of signal the crew begins treatment, then calls the surgeon as soon as possible. This is a 2001 rule. No current public NASA or ESA rule was found. No public NASA or ESA procedure says what a crew should do for an eye injury when the ground cannot answer. Looked in: OCHMO technical briefs index, NASA HRP 2017 in-flight medical conditions evidence report, Suh et al. and Meer et al. (npj Microgravity), public 2015 ISS medical kit checklist.
firstAidThatNeedsNoGround: Keep flushing a chemical eye injury for at least 15 minutes.
Leave a stuck object in place and loosely cover both eyes.
Record each vision check with the time.
Send the case as soon as the link returns.

proposedKeys.reason: Already proposed in new-measurement-keys.csv (section 3). Record one value per eye. Not in keys.ts yet, so the vision tests have no inputKey.

candidateItemNotes: kit-white-hypromellose is listed for dry eyes in the 2015 ISS kit list. Suh et al. list Hypromellose (Natures Tears) as a corneal abrasion item and say artificial tears may rinse minor particle abrasions. The eye chart and eyewash goggles are equipment, not consumables, so they are listed in equipmentIds (equipment.json ids eq-eye-chart and eq-eyewash), not in candidateItemIds.
gaps: No source we found says whether the onboard eye chart is a near or a distance chart. equipment.json names it a near vision card held at about 40 cm; check that with the Kit researcher before the app gives a distance.
No public source shows the eyewash goggles are still on board after 2015. The newest sources are the 2015 kit list and older ISS procedures.
The current ISS eye procedures are not public. This card uses the 2001 ISS checklist, peer reviewed reviews and MedlinePlus.
